what_it_does: Every computing system has a carbon footprint with two components: operational carbon (the electricity consumed while running) and embodied carbon (the greenhouse gases emitted during manufacturing of the chips, circuit boards, and packaging). Hardware designers face tradeoffs between these two: a more powerful chip runs workloads faster (less operational carbon per task) but costs more carbon to manufacture. CORDOBA proposes a single number — called the total Carbon Delay Product, or tCDP — that multiplies a system's total lifecycle carbon by how long it takes to complete a task, analogous to the energy-delay product that chip designers have long used to balance power against performance. Using this metric, the paper builds a framework that sweeps over a large space of hardware design choices (number of processor cores, memory configuration, whether to use traditional flat chips or a newer 3D-stacked design that places memory directly on top of logic) and prunes away options that are clearly worse than alternatives on both carbon and speed, cutting the search space by up to 98%. Two real processor configurations are studied, finding that halving core count and using 3D chip integration can improve the carbon-efficiency metric.
